An invertible real map preserves orientation when its determinant is positive and reverses ori-
entation when it is negative; its absolute determinant is the volume scale. This condition alone
does not imply orthogonality. Every planar orthogonal map is a rotation or a reflection: a re-
flection has eigenvalues 1, −1 and trace zero, and its fixed eigenspace is the reflecting line.

question.text:
First reflect in the line making angle π/6 with the positive x-axis, then reflect in the line mak-
ing angle π/3. What is the resulting map?
(A) Rotation by −π/3
(B) Rotation by π/6
(C) Rotation by π/3
(D) Reflection in angle π/4
(E) The identity

solution.text:
The composition rotates by twice the angle from the first reflecting line to the second:
2(π/3 − π/6) = π/3 counterclockwise.

question.text:
A real orthogonal 2 × 2 matrix has trace one. Which description is forced?
(A) Reflection in a line through the origin
(B) Rotation by π/3 or −π/3, modulo 2π
(C) Rotation by π/3 only
(D) Rotation by 2π/3 or −2π/3
(E) A length-changing map of determinant one

solution.text:
A planar orthogonal matrix with determinant −1 is a reflection and has trace zero. Thus
this matrix is a rotation, with 2 cos θ = 1. Its angle is θ = ±π/3 modulo 2π; trace alone
does not distinguish the direction of rotation.
